claims.claim: DMD-4::GFP fluorescence is first detectable in mid-embryonic development.
claims.source: DMD-4::GFP fluorescence is first detectable in mid-embryonic development, with a pattern that is restricted to all the pharyngeal and the hmc cells described above.
claims.evidence: This is based on developmental time-course microscopy observations.

claims.claim: Onset of DMD-4::GFP expression in the non-pharyngeal nervous system is first observed at around hatching.
claims.source: Onset of expression in the non-pharyngeal nervous system is first observed at around hatching in the same set of head and tail sensory neurons as observed in the adult stage, including the phasmid neurons PHA and PHB.
claims.evidence: This is based on developmental time-course microscopy observations.

claims.claim: DMD-4::GFP protein starts to disappear from PHA and PHB in the male at the L4 to adult molt, but not in the hermaphrodite.
claims.source: During larval development, dmd-4::gfp expression is the same in both sexes until the L4 to adult molt when DMD-4::GFP protein starts to disappear from PHA and PHB in the male, but not the hermaphrodite (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by developmental time-course microscopy data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Sexually dimorphic dmd-4::gfp expression in the adult PHA and PHB neurons is the result of male-specific downregulation of dmd-4::gfp from these neurons.
claims.source: We conclude that sexually dimorphic dmd-4::gfp expression in the adult PHA and PHB neurons is the result of male-specific downregulation of dmd-4::gfp from these neurons.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the developmental time-course data showing loss of expression in males but not hermaphrodites.

claims.claim: The dmd-4(ot933) putative null allele results in highly penetrant embryonic lethality.
claims.source: This putative null allele (ot933) results in highly penetrant embryonic lethality (Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantification of embryonic lethality shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: The dmd-4(tm1951) deletion allele results in lethality.
claims.source: A deletion allele generated by the C. elegans knockout consortium (tm1951), that eliminates parts of the DM domain, also results in lethality.
claims.evidence: This is a direct observation of the phenotype of this allele.

claims.claim: Null mutant dmd-4 animals that escape embryonic lethality are scrawny and display a stuffed anterior intestine.
claims.source: Null mutant animals that escape embryonic lethality are scrawny and display a stuffed anterior intestine (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by microscopy and quantification shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B.

claims.claim: The hmc fails to express arg-1::gfp in dmd-4 mutants.
claims.source: The stuffed anterior intestine may relate to developmental defects of the hmc, which fail to express a cell fate marker (arg-1::gfp) in dmd-4 mutants (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: The dmd-4(ot896) allele results in no embryonic lethality.
claims.source: Another deletion allele that we generated using CRISPR/Cas9 leaves the DNA binding domain unaffected, but deletes other domains of the protein (DMA domain and EH1 domain)(Figure 2A), but this allele (ot896) results in no embryonic lethality.
claims.evidence: This is a direct observation of the phenotype of this allele.

claims.claim: The third intron of the dmd-4 locus contains the cis-regulatory information for all nervous system expression.
claims.source: Through the fusion of individual segments of the dmd-4 locus to gfp, we identified the third intron of the dmd-4 locus as containing the cis-regulatory information for all nervous system expression (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by transgenic reporter assays shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: In dmd-4(ot957ot935) animals, dmd-4::gfp expression is lost in all head and tail neurons at all developmental stages.
claims.source: Using CRISPR/Cas9 genome engineering, we deleted this enhancer in the context of the dmd-4::gfp allele (dmd-4(ot957ot935)), and indeed found that in these animals dmd-4::gfp expression was lost in all head and tail neurons at all developmental stages, but unaffected in the pharynx and hmc (Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: dmd-4(ot957ot935) mutants show none of the lethality or intestinal stuffing phenotypes associated with removal of the gene from all tissues.
claims.source: Most importantly, dmd-4(ot957ot935) mutants showed none of the lethality or intestinal stuffing phenotypes associated with removal of the gene from all tissues (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B), allowing us to characterize the function of dmd-4 in the nervous system.
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantification shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B.

claims.claim: All head sensory neurons and phasmid neurons are generated in dmd-4(ot957ot935) mutant hermaphrodites.
claims.source: We found no evidence of defects in general neuronal specification or morphology; all head sensory neurons as well as the phasmid neurons were generated in dmd-4(ot957ot935) mutant hermaphrodites and had a normal appearance of axon and dendrite morphologies (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: Neurons in dmd-4(ot957ot935) mutant hermaphrodites have a normal appearance of axon and dendrite morphologies.
claims.source: We found no evidence of defects in general neuronal specification or morphology; all head sensory neurons as well as the phasmid neurons were generated in dmd-4(ot957ot935) mutant hermaphrodites and had a normal appearance of axon and dendrite morphologies (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: There is no loss or misexpression of neurotransmitter identity, neuropeptides, and receptors in the amphid and phasmid neurons of dmd-4(ot957ot935) mutant animals.
claims.source: Furthermore, we examined transgenic reporters for neurotransmitter identity, neuropeptides, and receptors, and found no loss or misexpression of these genes in the amphid and phasmid neurons of dmd-4(ot957ot935) mutant animals (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: Behaviors associated with the function of head amphid sensory neurons appear unaffected in dmd-4(ot957ot935) mutant animals.
claims.source: Lastly, behaviors associated with the function of head amphid sensory neurons also appear unaffected (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is supported by behavioral assay data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: PHA and PHB neurons display dimorphic synaptic connections to neurons that are shared between the two sexes.
claims.source: Not only do both the PHA and PHB neurons generate synaptic connections to male-specific neurons, but they also display dimorphic synaptic connections to neurons that are shared between the two sexes (Figure 1C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 1C.

claims.claim: Juvenile stages of C. elegans exhibit non-dimorphic 'sex-hybrid' connectivity in phasmid neurons.
claims.source: We have previously used in vivo synapse labeling techniques, GRASP (GFP-Reconstitution Across Synaptic Partners)(Feinberg et al., 2008) and iBLINC (Desbois et al., 2015), to show that juvenile stages exhibit non-dimorphic 'sex-hybrid' connectivity and that during sexual maturation, some synapses are then pruned, while others are maintained (Figure 3A; Oren-Suissa et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by GRASP and iBLINC data from a previous study and shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: During sexual maturation, some phasmid neuron synapses are pruned, while others are maintained.
claims.source: We have previously used in vivo synapse labeling techniques, GRASP (GFP-Reconstitution Across Synaptic Partners)(Feinberg et al., 2008) and iBLINC (Desbois et al., 2015), to show that juvenile stages exhibit non-dimorphic 'sex-hybrid' connectivity and that during sexual maturation, some synapses are then pruned, while others are maintained (Figure 3A; Oren-Suissa et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by GRASP and iBLINC data from a previous study and shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: Synaptic maintenance in phasmid neurons is not dependent on sex-specific patterns of neuronal activity.
claims.source: Unlike many pruning/maintenance events during nervous system development in other animal species (Katz and Callaway, 1992; Katz and Shatz, 1996; Morgan et al., 2011; Vonhoff and Keshishian, 2017), this synaptic maintenance is not dependent on sex-specific patterns of neuronal activity.
claims.evidence: This is supported by genetic silencing experiments and unc-13 mutant analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Genetic silencing of the phasmid neurons does not affect sexually dimorphic synapse pruning/maintenance.
claims.source: We arrived at this conclusion by genetic silencing of the phasmid neurons or reducing synaptic signaling in unc-13 mutant animals, neither of which affects sexually dimorphic synapse pruning/maintenance (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by GRASP data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Reducing synaptic signaling in unc-13 mutant animals does not affect sexually dimorphic synapse pruning/maintenance.
claims.source: We arrived at this conclusion by genetic silencing of the phasmid neurons or reducing synaptic signaling in unc-13 mutant animals, neither of which affects sexually dimorphic synapse pruning/maintenance (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by GRASP data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: The hermaphrodite-specific connections between PHB>AVA and PHA>AVG are unaffected in dmd-4(ot957ot935) mutants.
claims.source: While hermaphrodite-specific synaptic connections (between PHA>AVG and PHB>AVA) are unaffected in dmd-4 mutants (Figure 3A,B, Figure 3—figure supplement 2), male-specific synapses (PHB>AVG) failed to be pruned in hermaphrodite dmd-4 mutants (Figure 3A,C, Figure 3—figure supplement 2; Oren-Suissa et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by GRASP data shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: Male-specific synapses (PHB>AVG) fail to be pruned in hermaphrodite dmd-4 mutants.
claims.source: While hermaphrodite-specific synaptic connections (between PHA>AVG and PHB>AVA) are unaffected in dmd-4 mutants (Figure 3A,B, Figure 3—figure supplement 2), male-specific synapses (PHB>AVG) failed to be pruned in hermaphrodite dmd-4 mutants (Figure 3A,C, Figure 3—figure supplement 2; Oren-Suissa et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by GRASP data shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: Wild-type males display more PHA synaptic outputs than wild-type hermaphrodites.
claims.source: Transgenic animals show the predicted sexual dimorphism based on electron micrographic reconstruction of PHA synaptic connectivity, with wild-type males displaying more synaptic outputs than wild-type hermaphrodites (Figure 1C, Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 2; Cook et al., 2019; Jarrell et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is supported by RAB-3 puncta quantification and electron microscopy data.

claims.claim: In dmd-4(ot957ot935) mutant animals, the sexual dimorphism of PHA synaptic output is lost.
claims.source: In dmd-4(ot957ot935) mutant animals this sexual dimorphism is also lost, corroborating the notion that synapses fail to be pruned (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is supported by RAB-3 puncta quantification shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: Expressing dmd-4 cDNA under the control of a PHB-specific promoter rescues the PHB>AVG synaptic pruning defect.
claims.source: We rescued the PHB>AVG synaptic pruning defect by expressing dmd-4 cDNA under the control of a PHB-specific promoter, confirming the cell-autonomous role of dmd-4 in the presynaptic neuron to control sex-specific synaptic pruning (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is supported by GRASP data from rescue experiments shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: dmd-4 functions in the phasmid neurons to promote pruning of phasmid synaptic connections in hermaphrodite animals during sexual maturation.
claims.source: Taken together our results indicate that dmd-4 functions in the phasmid neurons to promote pruning of phasmid synaptic connections in hermaphrodite animals during sexual maturation.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the mutant phenotype and rescue data.

claims.claim: In larval animals, the phasmid neurons function to mediate chemosensory avoidance behavior.
claims.source: In larval animals, the phasmid neurons function to mediate chemosensory avoidance behavior (Hilliard et al., 2002; Zou et al., 2017), a functional output which is maintained in adult hermaphrodites, but lost in adult males (Oren-Suissa et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claims.claim: Chemosensory avoidance behavior mediated by phasmid neurons is maintained in adult hermaphrodites, but lost in adult males.
claims.source: In larval animals, the phasmid neurons function to mediate chemosensory avoidance behavior (Hilliard et al., 2002; Zou et al., 2017), a functional output which is maintained in adult hermaphrodites, but lost in adult males (Oren-Suissa et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claims.claim: dmd-4 mutants exhibit no defects in SDS avoidance in juvenile stages, before sexual maturation.
claims.source: dmd-4 mutants exhibit no defects in SDS avoidance in juvenile stages, before sexual maturation (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by behavioral assay data shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: As adults, dmd-4 mutant hermaphrodites display a partial masculinization of SDS avoidance behavior.
claims.source: However, as adults, these animals display a partial masculinization of SDS avoidance behavior, such that mutant hermaphrodites were less responsive to the noxious stimulus, although still intermediate relative to control adult males (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by behavioral assay data shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: In ceh-14 null mutants, dmd-4::gfp expression is selectively lost in the phasmid neurons in both sexes during larval stages and in the adult stage in hermaphrodites.
claims.source: We find that in ceh-14 null mutants, dmd-4::gfp expression is selectively lost in the phasmid neurons in both sexes during larval stages and in the adult stage in hermaphrodites (Figure 5A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: dmd-4(ot957ot935) mutant hermaphrodites display masculinization of SDS avoidance behavior.
claims.source: This is also consistent with the observation that dmd-4(ot957ot935) mutant hermaphrodites display masculinization of SDS avoidance behavior (Figure 4A), a phenotype observed in ceh-14 mutant hermaphrodites (Oren-Suissa et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by behavioral assay data shown in Figure 4A and citation to prior work.

claims.claim: ceh-14 mutant hermaphrodites display masculinization of SDS avoidance behavior.
claims.source: This is also consistent with the observation that dmd-4(ot957ot935) mutant hermaphrodites display masculinization of SDS avoidance behavior (Figure 4A), a phenotype observed in ceh-14 mutant hermaphrodites (Oren-Suissa et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claims.claim: Constitutive, panneuronal expression of LIN-41 maintains DMD-4 in the adult male phasmids.
claims.source: We generated transgenic animals that constitutively express LIN-41 in the nervous system and asked whether ectopically maintaining LIN-41 throughout all larval stages to adulthood is sufficient to maintain DMD-4 expression in the adult male phasmids. Indeed, we found that DMD-4 was ectopically maintained in these transgenic male animals (Figure 5B), demonstrating that the heterochronic pathway functions to regulate the timing of DMD-4 degradation.
claims.evidence: This is supported by microscopy data from transgenic animals shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: The heterochronic pathway functions to regulate the timing of DMD-4 degradation.
claims.source: We generated transgenic animals that constitutively express LIN-41 in the nervous system and asked whether ectopically maintaining LIN-41 throughout all larval stages to adulthood is sufficient to maintain DMD-4 expression in the adult male phasmids. Indeed, we found that DMD-4 was ectopically maintained in these transgenic male animals (Figure 5B), demonstrating that the heterochronic pathway functions to regulate the timing of DMD-4 degradation.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the LIN-41 overexpression data shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: Genetic removal of tra-1 in tra-1(e1099) XX pseudomales leads to a downregulation of DMD-4 expression in hermaphrodite phasmid neurons at the adult stage.
claims.source: We found that genetic removal of tra-1, in tra-1(e1099) XX pseudomales, leads to a downregulation of DMD-4 expression in hermaphrodite phasmid neurons at the adult stage (Figure 5C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 5C.

claims.claim: Force-expression of an engineered, activated version of the TRA-1 protein in the phasmid neurons of both sexes results in ectopic DMD-4 expression in male phasmid neurons.
claims.source: Conversely, force-expression of an engineered, activated version of the TRA-1 protein which escapes protein degradation (Schvarzstein and Spence, 2006) in the phasmid neurons of both sexes results in ectopic DMD-4 expression in male phasmid neurons (Figure 5D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by microscopy data from transgenic animals shown in Figure 5D.

claims.claim: The transcriptional regulator TRA-1 normally acts to promote DMD-4::GFP expression in hermaphrodite phasmid neurons upon sexual maturation.
claims.source: We conclude that the transcriptional regulator TRA-1 normally acts to promote DMD-4::GFP expression in hermaphrodite phasmid neurons upon sexual maturation, while its absence in adult male phasmids results in DMD-4 loss.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the tra-1 mutant and overexpression data.

claims.claim: The absence of TRA-1 in adult male phasmids results in DMD-4 loss.
claims.source: We conclude that the transcriptional regulator TRA-1 normally acts to promote DMD-4::GFP expression in hermaphrodite phasmid neurons upon sexual maturation, while its absence in adult male phasmids results in DMD-4 loss.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the tra-1 mutant and overexpression data.

claims.claim: The transcriptional reporter containing the nervous system enhancer for dmd-4 expression is expressed in the phasmid neurons of both adult hermaphrodite and adult male animals.
claims.source: However, in the context of our analysis of the cis-regulatory control regions of dmd-4 expression, we noted that the transcriptional reporter containing the nervous system enhancer for dmd-4 expression (Figure 2B), was expressed in the phasmid neurons of both adult hermaphrodite and adult male animals (Figure 6A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 6A.

claims.claim: The regulatory information generating DMD-4 sexual dimorphism is not encoded on the transcriptional level.
claims.source: This suggested that the regulatory information generating DMD-4 sexual dimorphism is not encoded on the transcriptional level.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that the transcriptional reporter is not dimorphic.

claims.claim: Expressing gfp tagged dmd-4 cDNA with a heterologous 3' UTR under control of a non-dimorphic PHA-specific and PHB-specific promoter shows dimorphic GFP fluorescence in the phasmid neurons.
claims.source: To define the potential mechanism of posttranscriptional regulation, we expressed gfp tagged dmd-4 cDNA with a heterologous 3' UTR under control of a non-dimorphic PHA-specific and PHB-specific promoter. In transgenic animals, these constructs show dimorphic GFP fluorescence in the phasmid neurons, identical to the endogenous DMD-4::GFP expression pattern (Figure 6B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by microscopy data from transgenic animals shown in Figure 6B.

claims.claim: The dmd-4 cDNA alone confers male-specific downregulation.
claims.source: Since the dmd-4 cDNA alone confers male-specific downregulation, sexually dimorphic DMD-4 presence may be controlled on the level of stability/degradation of the protein.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that the cDNA with heterologous UTR is still dimorphic.

claims.claim: Sexually dimorphic DMD-4 presence may be controlled on the level of stability/degradation of the protein.
claims.source: Since the dmd-4 cDNA alone confers male-specific downregulation, sexually dimorphic DMD-4 presence may be controlled on the level of stability/degradation of the protein.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that the cDNA with heterologous UTR is still dimorphic.

claims.claim: The DMA domain shows sequence similarity to CUE domains.
claims.source: Pairwise alignments of profile hidden Markov models using HHsearch (Soding, 2005) reveals that the DMA domain shows sequence similarity to CUE domains (for coupling of ubiquitin to ER degradation), a subtype of the ubiquitin-associated (UBA) family of domains (Kang et al., 2003; Figure 7A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by computational sequence analysis shown in Figure 7A.

claims.claim: CUE domains are a subtype of the ubiquitin-associated (UBA) family of domains.
claims.source: Pairwise alignments of profile hidden Markov models using HHsearch (Soding, 2005) reveals that the DMA domain shows sequence similarity to CUE domains (for coupling of ubiquitin to ER degradation), a subtype of the ubiquitin-associated (UBA) family of domains (Kang et al., 2003; Figure 7A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claims.claim: The DMA domain contains three alpha-helices.
claims.source: The DMA domain contains three alpha-helices; by analogy with CUE domains, helices 1 and 3 would be expected to form a binding surface for direct non-covalent contact with ubiquitin.
claims.evidence: This is based on the homology model shown in Figure 7B.

claims.claim: Helices 1 and 3 of the DMA domain would be expected to form a binding surface for direct non-covalent contact with ubiquitin.
claims.source: The DMA domain contains three alpha-helices; by analogy with CUE domains, helices 1 and 3 would be expected to form a binding surface for direct non-covalent contact with ubiquitin.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on analogy with CUE domains and the homology model.

claims.claim: The C. elegans DMD-4 DMA domain binds to monoubiquitin.
claims.source: SPR binding analysis of the C. elegans dmd-4 and human Dmrt3 DMA domains shows that both bind to monoubiquitin, and this binding is lost in the L31R mutation (see panel A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by SPR binding data shown in Figure 7C.

claims.claim: The human DMRT3 DMA domain binds to monoubiquitin.
claims.source: SPR binding analysis of the C. elegans dmd-4 and human Dmrt3 DMA domains shows that both bind to monoubiquitin, and this binding is lost in the L31R mutation (see panel A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by SPR binding data shown in Figure 7C.

claims.claim: The L31R mutation in the DMA domain abolishes binding to monoubiquitin.
claims.source: SPR binding analysis of the C. elegans dmd-4 and human Dmrt3 DMA domains shows that both bind to monoubiquitin, and this binding is lost in the L31R mutation (see panel A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by SPR binding data shown in Figure 7C.

claims.claim: The DMD-4 DMA domain bound monoubiquitin with an affinity of ~400 µM.
claims.source: The DMD-4 DMA domain bound monoubiquitin with an affinity of ~400 µM, which is similar to known affinities for CUE-ubiquitin binding (Hurley et al., 2006; Figure 7C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by SPR binding data shown in Figure 7C.

claims.claim: The affinity of the DMD-4 DMA domain for ubiquitin is similar to known affinities for CUE-ubiquitin binding.
claims.source: The DMD-4 DMA domain bound monoubiquitin with an affinity of ~400 µM, which is similar to known affinities for CUE-ubiquitin binding (Hurley et al., 2006; Figure 7C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by comparison to literature values.

claims.claim: The DMA domain of DMD-4 behaves as a monomer.
claims.source: Testing whether the DMA domain of DMD-4 may display the same feature, we used size exclusion chromatography with multi-angle static light scattering (SEC-MALS). We found that the DMD-4 DMA domain behaves as a monomer (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by SEC-MALS data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: The in vitro binding of the L31R mutated DMA domain to ubiquitin was disrupted, with the affinity reduced from 404 µM to >3 mM.
claims.source: As expected, the in vitro binding of the mutated DMA domain to ubiquitin was disrupted, with the affinity of mutant DMD-4 DMA for ubiquitin reduced from 404 µ﻿M to >3 mM (Figure 7C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by SPR binding data shown in Figure 7C.

claims.claim: In dmd-4(ot990ot935) animals, DMD-4 expression is lost in the phasmid neurons in both sexes and at all stages of development.
claims.source: Much to our surprise, we observed the exact opposite result; we find that in dmd-4(ot990ot935) animals, DMD-4 expression is lost in the phasmid neurons in both sexes and at all stages of development (Figure 7D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 7D.

claims.claim: In dmd-4(ot990ot935) animals, DMD-4 expression in the head sensory neurons is lost in both sexes of all stages.
claims.source: Expression in the head sensory neurons was also lost, again in both sexes of all stages.
claims.evidence: This is based on microscopy observations of the ot990 mutant.

claims.claim: The ot990 allele results in defective pruning on the PHB>AVG synaptic connection in hermaphrodites.
claims.source: Consistent with the phenotype of the ot957 null allele, the ot990 allele also results in defective pruning on the PHB>AVG synaptic connection in hermaphrodites (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).

results.result: DMD-4 is one of ten DMRT proteins in C. elegans, with DMD-4 and DMD-5 being phylogenetically conserved in vertebrates. Neither the expression nor function of DMD-4 had been previously described.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C3 establish the phylogenetic context and novelty of the study. C1 and C2 are supported by citations to prior phylogenetic analyses (Volff et al., 2003; Wexler et al., 2014), and C3 establishes the novelty of the current work. These claims provide appropriate background context.

results.result: DMD-4::GFP is expressed in a sexually dimorphic manner in adult phasmid neurons (PHA and PHB) of hermaphrodites but not males, and in a non-dimorphic manner in head sensory neurons and pharyngeal/alimentary tissues. The sexual dimorphism results from male-specific downregulation during the L4-to-adult transition.
results.evaluation: Claims C4-C15 describe the expression pattern of DMD-4::GFP based on microscopy of a CRISPR-tagged endogenous locus (Figure 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 1). The developmental time-course data (C12-C14) supports the conclusion that dimorphism arises from male-specific downregulation (C15). The data are internally consistent and well-documented.

results.result: Null alleles of dmd-4 (ot933, tm1951) cause highly penetrant embryonic lethality and stuffed anterior intestine in escapers, while a deletion preserving the DNA-binding domain (ot896) shows no lethality.
results.evaluation: Claims C16-C20 describe phenotypes of different dmd-4 alleles. The embryonic lethality of ot933 is quantified in Figure 2A with statistical analysis. The stuffed intestine phenotype (C18) and hmc defects (C19) are documented in Figure 2—figure supplement 1. The viability of ot896 (C20) demonstrates domain-specific requirements.

results.result: The third intron of dmd-4 contains the cis-regulatory element for nervous system expression. Deletion of this enhancer (ot957ot935 allele) eliminates neuronal expression while preserving pharyngeal expression and viability.
results.evaluation: Claims C21-C23 describe the generation of a nervous system-specific knockout. C21 is supported by transgenic reporter assays (Figure 2B), C22 by microscopy of the engineered allele (Figure 2C), and C23 by quantification showing no lethality or intestinal defects (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B). This elegant genetic approach enables tissue-specific functional analysis.

results.result: The dmd-4(ot957ot935) nervous system-specific mutant shows normal neuronal specification, morphology, neurotransmitter identity, and head sensory neuron behaviors.
results.evaluation: Claims C24-C27 establish that dmd-4 is not required for general neuronal development. Multiple cell-type markers (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A) and chemotaxis assays (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B) support these conclusions. This is important for interpreting subsequent synaptic connectivity defects as specific rather than secondary to developmental abnormalities.

results.result: Phasmid neurons display sexually dimorphic synaptic connectivity. Juvenile stages exhibit non-dimorphic 'sex-hybrid' connectivity that is sculpted during sexual maturation through activity-independent synaptic pruning and maintenance.
results.evaluation: Claims C28-C33 establish the developmental context for synaptic dimorphism. C28 is supported by electron microscopy data (Figure 1C, Cook et al., 2019; Jarrell et al., 2012). C29-C30 are supported by prior GRASP/iBLINC studies (Oren-Suissa et al., 2016). C31-C33 demonstrate activity-independence using genetic silencing and unc-13 mutants (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).

results.result: dmd-4 functions cell-autonomously in phasmid neurons to promote hermaphrodite-specific synaptic pruning. In dmd-4 mutants, male-specific synapses fail to be pruned in hermaphrodites, while hermaphrodite-specific connections are unaffected.
results.evaluation: Claims C34-C39 describe the core synaptic phenotype. GRASP data (Figure 3A-C, Figure 3—figure supplement 2) show selective defects in pruning male-specific PHB>AVG synapses (C35) while hermaphrodite-specific connections are normal (C34). RAB-3 puncta quantification (C36-C37) corroborates the GRASP results. Cell-autonomous rescue (C38) confirms presynaptic function. Statistical analyses support all quantitative claims.

results.result: dmd-4 mutant hermaphrodites display partial masculinization of adult SDS avoidance behavior, with no defects in juvenile stages.
results.evaluation: Claims C40-C43 link synaptic defects to behavior. C40-C41 cite prior work establishing the behavioral assay. C42-C43 show stage-specific behavioral defects (Figure 4A) that parallel the timing of synaptic pruning defects. The behavioral phenotype is intermediate between wild-type hermaphrodites and males, consistent with incomplete masculinization. Statistical analysis supports the quantitative claims.

results.result: The terminal selector transcription factor CEH-14 is required for dmd-4 expression in phasmid neurons. Loss of ceh-14 phenocopies dmd-4 mutants in causing masculinization of SDS avoidance behavior.
results.evaluation: Claims C44-C46 establish spatial control of dmd-4 expression. C44 is supported by microscopy showing selective loss of DMD-4::GFP in phasmid neurons of ceh-14 mutants (Figure 5A). C45-C46 link this to behavior, with C46 citing prior work (Oren-Suissa et al., 2016). This places dmd-4 downstream of a known phasmid neuron specification factor.

results.result: Constitutive panneuronal expression of LIN-41 maintains DMD-4 in adult male phasmids, demonstrating that the heterochronic pathway regulates the timing of DMD-4 degradation.
results.evaluation: Claims C47-C48 establish temporal control via the heterochronic pathway. C47 is supported by microscopy of transgenic animals expressing LIN-41 (Figure 5B), showing ectopic DMD-4 maintenance in adult males. C48 is a reasonable inference from this gain-of-function experiment. The data directly demonstrate that LIN-41 is sufficient to prevent DMD-4 loss.

results.result: The sex determination transcription factor TRA-1 promotes DMD-4 expression in hermaphrodite phasmid neurons. Loss of tra-1 causes DMD-4 downregulation in hermaphrodites, while forced TRA-1 expression maintains DMD-4 in males.
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C52 establish sexual control via TRA-1. C49 is supported by microscopy of tra-1(e1099) pseudomales (Figure 5C). C50 is supported by transgenic expression of activated TRA-1 (Figure 5D). C51-C52 are reasonable inferences from these loss- and gain-of-function experiments. The bidirectional genetic manipulations provide strong support.

results.result: DMD-4 sexual dimorphism is not controlled transcriptionally but rather post-transcriptionally at the level of protein stability/degradation, as demonstrated by non-dimorphic transcriptional reporters and dimorphic cDNA expression.
results.evaluation: Claims C53-C57 establish post-transcriptional regulation. C53 shows the transcriptional reporter is expressed in both sexes (Figure 6A). C55 shows that cDNA with heterologous UTR still exhibits dimorphic expression (Figure 6B). C54, C56-C57 are logical inferences from these observations. This is a key mechanistic insight that redirects investigation toward protein-level regulation.

results.result: The DMA domain shows sequence similarity to CUE domains (ubiquitin-binding domains) and contains three alpha-helices, with helices 1 and 3 predicted to form a ubiquitin-binding surface.
results.evaluation: Claims C58-C61 establish the structural basis for ubiquitin binding. C58 is supported by HHsearch analysis (Figure 7A). C59 cites prior work on CUE domain classification. C60-C61 are based on homology modeling (Figure 7B). While homology models have inherent uncertainty, the prediction is reasonable given the sequence similarity and is subsequently validated experimentally.

results.result: The DMA domains of C. elegans DMD-4 and human DMRT3 bind monoubiquitin with ~400 μM affinity, similar to CUE domains. The L31R mutation abolishes binding. The DMD-4 DMA domain behaves as a monomer.
results.evaluation: Claims C62-C68 provide biochemical validation of ubiquitin binding. SPR data (Figure 7C) demonstrate binding of both DMD-4 and DMRT3 DMA domains to ubiquitin (C62-C63, C65) with affinities comparable to CUE domains (C66). The L31R mutation disrupts binding (C64, C68), validating the predicted binding interface. SEC-MALS data (Figure 7—figure supplement 1) show the DMD-4 DMA domain is monomeric (C67). The biochemical data are rigorous and well-controlled.

results.result: Mutation of the ubiquitin-binding site (L31R, ot990 allele) causes loss of DMD-4 expression in neurons of both sexes at all stages, suggesting that ubiquitin binding is required for DMD-4 stability and that male-specific degradation may result from loss of ubiquitin-mediated stabilization.
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C73 demonstrate the functional importance of ubiquitin binding in vivo. Microscopy of the ot990 allele (Figure 7D) shows complete loss of neuronal DMD-4 in both sexes (C69-C70). GRASP data show synaptic pruning defects (C71, Figure 7—figure supplement 1A). C72 is a well-supported inference from these data. C73 is more speculative but reasonable. The unexpected result that disrupting ubiquitin binding causes protein loss (rather than preventing degradation) is a key finding.

results.result: The ubiquitin-binding mutation affects DMD-4 stability differently in different tissues and at different times: constitutively required in neurons, but only required in adulthood in pharyngeal/alimentary tissues. Multiple DMA domain mutations show similar phenotypes.
results.evaluation: Claims C74-C80 reveal tissue- and stage-specific requirements for ubiquitin binding. Microscopy of ot990 (Figure 7D) shows differential effects in neurons vs. pharynx (C74-C75). The lack of lethality or intestinal defects (C76-C77, Figure 2—figure supplement 2A,B) indicates sufficient pharyngeal function during development. Additional DMA mutations (ot966, ot967, ot968) show similar phenotypes (C78, Figure 7—figure supplement 1B). C79-C80 are reasonable inferences summarizing these complex spatiotemporal requirements.

results.result: The human DMRT3 DMA domain binds ubiquitin with similar affinity to DMD-4, but unlike DMD-4, the DMRT3 DMA domain can homodimerize.
results.evaluation: Claims C81-C82 extend the biochemical analysis to human DMRT3. SPR data (Figure 7C) demonstrate ubiquitin binding (C81). SEC-MALS data (Figure 7—figure supplement 1) show dimerization (C82). These data suggest conserved ubiquitin-binding function but divergent oligomerization properties between C. elegans and human proteins.

results.result: Human DMRT3::GFP expressed in C. elegans is not degraded in head neurons but is constitutively degraded in phasmid neurons of both sexes at all stages, without sexual or temporal control.
results.evaluation: Claims C83-C85 test whether human DMRT3 is subject to similar regulation in C. elegans. Microscopy of transgenic animals (Figure 7F) shows differential stability in head vs. phasmid neurons (C83-C84) but loss of sex-specific regulation (C85). This suggests partial conservation of regulatory mechanisms but incomplete recapitulation of endogenous DMD-4 regulation.

results.result: The phylogenetically conserved DMRT gene dmd-4 plays a critical role in sculpting sexually dimorphic synaptic connectivity by functioning sex-specifically in phasmid neurons to promote hermaphrodite-specific synapse pruning.
results.evaluation: Claims C86-C89 summarize the main findings. C86 is supported by phylogenetic analysis (C1-C2). C87-C89 are supported by the synaptic connectivity data (C34-C39) and expression data (C4-C15). This is a well-supported summary of the core biological findings.

results.result: DMD-4 differs from other DMRT proteins (DMD-5, DMD-11) in three ways: it promotes synapse maintenance rather than pruning, functions presynaptically rather than postsynaptically, and is hermaphrodite-specific rather than male-specific.
results.evaluation: Claims C90-C93 compare DMD-4 to other DMRT proteins. C90 is supported by the synaptic data (C35). C91-C92 cite prior work on DMD-5/DMD-11. C93 is supported by the rescue experiments (C38). These comparisons highlight the distinct function of DMD-4 among C. elegans DMRT proteins.

results.result: DMD-4 is expressed specifically in hermaphrodites, contrasting with the male-specific expression of all other dimorphically expressed C. elegans DMRT proteins (DMD-5, DMD-11, MAB-3, MAB-23, DMD-3).
results.evaluation: Claims C94-C96 emphasize the unique sexual specificity of DMD-4. C94 is supported by expression data (C4-C15). C95-C96 cite prior work. This establishes DMD-4 as the first hermaphrodite-specific DMRT protein identified in C. elegans, which is conceptually important.

results.result: dmd-4 is required for viability due to non-dimorphic functions in the feeding organ. This function is conserved in dmd-4 orthologs (DMRT93B in arthropods, Dmrt3 in vertebrates), with mouse Dmrt3 knockouts dying from feeding defects.
results.evaluation: Claims C97-C99 establish conserved non-dimorphic functions. C97 is supported by the lethality and intestinal phenotypes (C16-C19). C98-C99 cite prior work on orthologs. This demonstrates that dmd-4 has both sexually dimorphic neuronal functions and conserved non-dimorphic developmental functions.

results.result: Sex-specific transcription factor degradation has been observed for TRA-1 in C. elegans and Lola in Drosophila, indicating this is not an unprecedented mechanism.
results.evaluation: Claims C100-C101 provide context by citing prior examples of sex-specific protein degradation. Both claims cite appropriate prior work (Schvarzstein and Spence, 2006; Sato et al., 2019). This contextualizes the DMD-4 findings within known regulatory mechanisms.

results.result: The DMA domain is an evolutionarily ancient domain that was characteristic of the three ancestral DMRT gene clusters, arose before eumetazoans, but has not been maintained in all extant DMRT clusters.
results.evaluation: Claims C102-C105 establish the evolutionary context of the DMA domain. C102 is based on phylogenetic analysis. C103-C105 cite prior phylogenetic work (Mawaribuchi et al., 2019; Wexler et al., 2014). This establishes the ancient origin and variable retention of the DMA domain across evolution.

results.result: In C. elegans, dmd-4 is the only gene encoding a DMA domain, which is required for protein stability and binds monoubiquitin. Human DMRT3 also undergoes posttranslational regulation in worms, suggesting conserved molecular function.
results.evaluation: Claims C106-C110 summarize the molecular findings. C106 is based on genome analysis. C107-C108 are supported by the mutant and biochemical data (C69-C72, C62-C68). C109 is supported by the DMRT3 expression data (C83-C85). C110 is a reasonable inference from the combined data on C. elegans and human proteins.

results.result: CUE domains have diverse regulatory functions through ubiquitin association. Some non-covalent ubiquitin-binding domains stabilize proteins, as exemplified by yeast Met4, where the ubiquitin-binding domain prevents degradation.
results.evaluation: Claims C111-C114 provide mechanistic context by citing prior work on CUE domains and ubiquitin-mediated protein stabilization. All claims cite appropriate literature (Bagola et al., 2013; Chen et al., 2006; Davies et al., 2003; Prag et al., 2003; Flick et al., 2006; Heessen et al., 2005; Heinen et al., 2011, 2010). The Met4 example is particularly relevant as a precedent for the proposed DMD-4 mechanism.

results.result: By analogy to Met4, ubiquitin binding to DMD-4 may prevent protein degradation.
results.evaluation: Claim C115 is explicitly presented as a hypothesis based on analogy to Met4. While the analogy is reasonable given the similar phenotypes (loss of ubiquitin binding causes protein degradation), the actual mechanism by which ubiquitin binding stabilizes DMD-4 is not demonstrated. The claim is appropriately tentative but requires further experimental validation.

results.result: Ubiquitin-dependent stabilization of DMD-4 is susceptible to three parameters: sexual identity, cell-type, and developmental time. In wild-type animals, DMD-4 is only degraded in male phasmid neurons at a specific developmental stage.
results.evaluation: Claims C116-C119 synthesize the spatiotemporal regulation of DMD-4. C116 is an inference from the combined data. C117-C119 are directly supported by the expression data (C4-C15, C69-C80). This synthesis effectively captures the complex regulation of DMD-4 stability.

results.result: The DMD-4/ubiquitin interaction may be dynamically controlled in phasmid neurons, with destabilization as the default state that is antagonized by LIN-41 in juveniles and TRA-1 in adult hermaphrodites. Forced expression of either factor prevents degradation in adult males.
results.evaluation: Claims C120-C124 propose a model for dynamic regulation. C120-C121 are speculative but reasonable hypotheses based on the ot990 phenotype (C69-C73). C122 is a well-supported inference from the LIN-41 data (C47-C48). C123 is speculative but consistent with all data. C124 is directly supported by the transgenic experiments (C47, C50). While some aspects are speculative, the model is well-grounded in the experimental data.

results.result: Different tissues show different requirements for ubiquitin-mediated DMD-4 stabilization: head neurons always require it, while pharynx/hmc only require it in adulthood.
results.evaluation: Claims C125-C127 describe tissue-specific differences in regulation. C125 is an inference from the constitutive loss of DMD-4 in head neurons of ot990 mutants (C70). C126 is speculative but reasonable. C127 is a well-supported inference from the stage-specific loss in pharynx/hmc (C74-C75). These claims effectively capture the complexity of tissue-specific regulation.

results.result: Different C. elegans DMRT proteins use similar regulatory pathways (terminal selectors, TRA-1, LIN-41) but in fundamentally different ways. For mab-3/dmd-3, regulation is transcriptional and post-transcriptional (mRNA level); for dmd-4, regulation is post-translational (protein stability).
results.evaluation: Claims C128-C133 compare regulatory mechanisms across DMRT proteins. C128 is supported by the ceh-14 data (C44) and cites prior work. C129-C130 cite prior work on mab-3/dmd-3 regulation. C131-C132 are supported by the expression and stability data (C53-C57, C69-C80). C133 is a reasonable inference. This comparison effectively highlights the mechanistic novelty of dmd-4 regulation.
